messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Bounmy Phommasack is a 72-year-old Laotian-American man who works as a nanny for a family in the suburbs of Sacramento, California. He is married, soft-spoken, and widely regarded by the family he works for as gentle and unflappable — a man who has devoted his later years to the care of young children. What they do not know is that Bounmy arrives at work each morning carrying the weight of something that happened inside his own home, in a marriage that preceded his current one, decades ago and yet, in the most important sense, not over at all.

For several years during his fifties, Bounmy was in a relationship with a woman whose rages were unpredictable and, at their worst, physical. The assault that brought him to the present moment of seeking help occurred on an evening when the apartment was dark — she had turned the lights off before she came at him, and he had not seen her approach. She struck him repeatedly, and at one point pinned him against the kitchen wall, her hands at his throat. He did not fight back. He had never fought back. When it was over he slid to the floor in the dark and remained there for a long time, unable to tell whether the danger had passed.

In the years that followed, Bounmy rebuilt his life with considerable outward success. He remarried, found work he loved, and said very little about what had happened. But the event had left residue that did not dissolve with time. He had come to understand the darkness as something that carried threat inside it — not symbolically, but as a felt physical fact. In the Sacramento house where he works, the children sometimes run ahead of him and switch off hallway lights as a game, and in those moments Bounmy's body responds before his mind can intervene. His heart hammers. His shoulders pull inward. He finds himself pressing his back against the nearest wall, arms slightly raised, his body arranging itself into the exact posture he held on the kitchen floor that night — not as a choice but as something his muscles remember without being asked.

When the memory surfaces fully, it does not feel like his own history. He describes it with a kind of bewildered distance, as though he is recounting something that happened to a man he once read about. And yet the terror that accompanies it is entirely his own, immediate and total, as raw as it was the first time. These two qualities — the sense that the memory belongs to a stranger, and the feeling that the danger it contains is happening now — coexist in him without resolution.

Bounmy cannot relax. Even in his own living room, with his wife nearby and every light on, something in him remains at attention. An unexpected movement — a grandchild darting into his peripheral vision, a colleague stepping quickly around a corner at the family's house — produces a full-body startle, a sharp intake of breath, hands raised. He is embarrassed by this and works to conceal it. He has also made a quiet rule for himself: he will not be angry. Not ever, not even when anger would be reasonable. He had come to believe that anger in any form — his own or anyone else's — is the edge of something catastrophic, and so he smooths it away before it can form. He absorbs the frustrations of his work, the ordinary irritations of marriage, without reaction, and the effort of this costs him more than anyone around him can see.

Over the past year, Bounmy has quietly reorganised his life to avoid anything he experiences as stressful, which has meant declining social invitations, stepping back from a community group at his temple, and finding reasons not to attend the children's school events when they are held in the evening. His wife has noticed the withdrawal and named it, gently, more than once.

It was she who finally persuaded him to seek help. What Bounmy is most afraid of, sitting in a therapist's office for the first time at seventy-two, is that the terror he carries is simply who he is now. What he hopes, with a tentativeness he can barely articulate, is that someone might tell him otherwise.
